title: Richer isn't better
hook: "I'm richer than you, so I'm better" doesn't follow (Enchiridion 44)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the two handles, and the one that can be carried. Your line was the other handle. Which conflict did you pick up differently? Day three hundred seventy-nine.

A twenty-year class reunion. Name tags, a slideshow, and a low hum of measuring. Who has the bigger house. Who has the better job title. Who still looks thirty. Nobody says the next step out loud, but it hangs in the room: so they're doing better than me. So I'm less than them. Epictetus heard the same hum in his own day, and in section forty-four he does something unexpected with it. He doesn't preach. He checks the logic. Today: richer isn't better.
screen: `A TWENTY-YEAR REUNION.` → `BIGGER HOUSE, BETTER TITLE.` → `RICHER ISN'T BETTER.`

segments.voice: First, two arguments that fail. I'm richer than you, so I'm better than you. I'm more eloquent than you, so I'm better than you. These don't follow, Epictetus says. The conclusion doesn't come out of the premise. Second, two arguments that work. I'm richer than you, so my property is greater than yours. I'm more eloquent than you, so my speech is better than yours. Those are fine. They compare like with like: money with money, speaking with speaking. Third, the hinge, and it's one short sentence. But you, he says, are neither property nor speech. That's the whole move. The comparison is real, but it's a comparison of things you have, or things you do. The jump from my things are bigger to I am better quietly assumes that you are your things. A Stoic says you're not. You're the one who uses them, who judges, who chooses. Fourth, why this is freeing in both directions. It takes the air out of the reunion bragging, of course. But it also takes the sting out of losing the comparison. Their house is bigger. Fine: their house is bigger. That says something true about two houses, and nothing at all about two people. You can admire someone's skill, or envy their savings, and still notice that it doesn't follow. And the same check works on the voice that says I'm worse at this, so I'm worth less. It doesn't follow either.
screen: `RICHER, SO BETTER? DOESN'T FOLLOW.` · `RICHER, SO MORE PROPERTY? FINE.` · `YOU ARE NEITHER PROPERTY NOR SPEECH.` · `IT FREES THE WINNER AND THE LOSER.` · then, large: `DOESN'T FOLLOW.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of one comparison that's been running in your head lately. Someone's salary, someone's body, someone's family, someone's follower count. Say the full sentence to yourself, including the hidden last step: they have more, so they're better than me. Now break it the way Epictetus does. They have more. True. So their things are more. True. So they are better? Doesn't follow. Rest there for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Richer isn't better. Epictetus checks the logic: more money means more property, not a better person. You are neither property nor speech. Today's word.
Your line: doesn't follow. Catch one bad comparison today, about someone else or yourself, and say it plainly: doesn't follow. Day three hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism sometimes catch comparisons that jump from 'they have more' to 'they are better' and correct the logic, as in Enchiridion 44.

myth: Epictetus says being rich is bad
he says richer means more property, which is fine. it just doesn't make you better.
section forty-four is built as a logic check
two arguments that fail, two that work, and the reason why.

fork.setup: at the reunion, an old classmate says: I make twice what you do, so I've done better than you. what does Epictetus say?
options: doesn't follow. twice the salary, yes; a better person, no.
find something you're better at, and say so.
fork.reveal: twice the money means twice the money. you are neither property nor speech, so the step to 'better' doesn't follow.

trapdoor: what you thought: money doesn't buy happiness.
what it means: comparing possessions or skills is fine, but jumping from 'more' to 'better person' is bad logic.
what a scholar hears: Enchiridion 44 is a lesson in Stoic logic: the conclusion must be about the same thing as the premise.

notes: Enchiridion 44 paraphrased: these reasonings are not coherent: I am richer, therefore better; more eloquent, therefore better. These are: I am richer, therefore my possessions are greater; more eloquent, therefore my speech is better. But you are neither possession nor speech. Confirm.
Original set to null: the Greek term for 'don't follow' (ἀσύνακτοι) was not used because its exact wording in Ench. 44 is unverified.
Editor review (2026-10-01): 'heard the same hum in Rome' changed to 'in his own day' (the handbook comes from his teaching at Nicopolis); removed 'you can feel it' and 'almost nobody'.
